Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The work is not a game or playful system; it is an empirical study (systematic review plus interviews) about avatar diversity, disability disclosure, and accessibility in existing commercial social VR platforms. The focus is on understanding and improving utilitarian aspects (representation, accessibility, disclosure control) rather than creating a fun-first experience. There is no co-design of a playful artifact with stakeholders; instead, they analyze current platforms and derive design implications, which aligns best with a mostly utility-first orientation.

        (1) unstructured play (i.e., no rules, making art),
        (2) semi-structured play (i.e., playground activities),
        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: The study involves participants using and customizing avatars within existing commercial social VR platforms, which are structured environments with provided interaction options but not rigid, win-oriented games. This aligns best with semi-structured play (2), similar to playground activities with available structures and affordances but open-ended goals.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The work is not a game but a review plus interview study about avatar design and disability disclosure in social VR. Social VR interactions and avatar customization are not structured as turns or phases; users act concurrently in a shared space. Among the given options, this most closely matches an entirely simultaneous design.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: The study focuses on commercial social VR platforms (e.g., Rec Room, VRChat, Horizon Worlds), which are real-time, co-present virtual environments where interaction and avatar use occur synchronously. There is no mention of turn-based or delayed/asynchronous mechanics; social VR by design is predominantly real-time communication and interaction, so the best fit is entirely synchronous.

        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),

reasoning: The work studies avatar design and disability disclosure in social VR platforms used as social media, not games. The interactions described are about self-presentation, identity, and accessibility in shared virtual spaces, with no mention of competition, scoring, or adversarial goals. Social VR is inherently cooperative/social rather than competitive, so the design context aligns best with an entirely collaborative setting.

        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),

There are no roles, turn structures, or mechanics that differentiate participants; all participants interact with avatar systems in essentially the same way.
